# Thalassemia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Red blood cell disorders > Thalassemia*

[Original Article Link](/library/tT0Xs2)

---

## Summary

Thalassemias are a group of hereditary <u>hemoglobin</u> disorders characterized by mutations on the α- or <u>β-globin</u> chains (resulting in alpha or <u>beta thalassemia</u>). Thalassemias can be further classified according to the specific <u>genotype</u>: the <u>α-chain</u> is coded by four <u>alleles</u>, resulting in four possible variants depending on the number of <u>alleles</u> affected, while the β-chain is coded by two <u>alleles</u>, resulting in two possible variants. The number of <u>alleles</u> affected is directly related to the severity of the disease (minor/intermedia/major). Thalassemia mutations are generally more frequent in areas where <u>malaria</u> is <u>endemic</u>; alpha thalassemias occur most commonly in individuals of Asian or African descent, whereas beta thalassemias are predominant in individuals of Mediterranean descent. The key feature in all forms of thalassemia is <u>microcytic hypochromic anemia</u> (which may be very mild in minor forms), but more severe forms may also manifest with <u>hemolysis</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, delay in growth and development, and skeletal deformities. The diagnostic workup for suspected thalassemia includes a <u>blood smear</u>, <u>hemoglobin electrophoresis</u>, <u>high-performance liquid chromatography</u> (<u>HPLC</u>), and, possibly, <u>genetic testing</u>. Minor forms of thalassemia usually require no treatment, while patients with thalassemia intermedia/major typically require regular <u>blood transfusions</u> and management of disease and treatment-related complications (e.g., <u>chelating agent</u> for <u>transfusion</u>-mediated <u>iron overload</u>).

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Beta thalassemia</u>: most commonly seen in people of Mediterranean descent

* <u>Alpha thalassemia</u>: most commonly seen in people of Asian and African descent

* Thalassemia provides partial resistance against <u>malaria</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> Alpha thalassemia is common in Asia and Africa.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### General [[1]](/library/AeYRYo)[[2]](/library/_eY5Yo)




* Cause: <u>gene mutations</u> 

* <u>Beta thalassemia</u>: usually due to <u>point mutations</u> in <u>promoter</u> sequences or <u>splicing</u> sites
* <u>β-globin</u> <u>locus</u> - short arm of <u>chromosome</u> 11

* <u>Alpha thalassemia</u>: usually due to deletion of at least one out of the four existing <u>alleles</u>
* The <u>α-globin</u> <u>gene</u> cluster is located on <u>chromosome</u> 16

* <u>Inheritance pattern</u>: <u>autosomal recessive</u>





### <u>Alpha thalassemia</u>




In a normal cell, the <u>α-globin</u> chains are coded by a total of four <u>alleles</u>.  Thus, there are four forms of the disease. The severity of <u>alpha thalassemia</u> depends on the number of defective <u>α-globin</u> <u>alleles</u>.




* Silent carrier (minima form): one defective <u>allele</u> (-α/αα)

* Alpha-thalassemia trait (minor form)

* Two defective <u>alleles</u> (-α/-α or --/αα)

* Cis-deletion is common among Asian populations, whereas trans-deletions are more common in African populations.

* Children of parents with a two-<u>gene</u> deletion in cis are at higher risk of developing <u>Hb Bart</u>.

* Hemoglobin H disease (intermedia form): three defective <u>alleles</u> (--/-α) → results in excessive production of pathologically altered <u>HbH</u>

* Hemoglobin Bart's disease (major form): four defective <u>alleles</u> (--/-‑) → results in excessive production of pathologically altered <u>Hb Bart</u> (consists of four γ-chains; γ-tetramers)





### <u>Beta thalassemia</u> [[3]](/library/CeYqao)[[4]](/library/xeYEao)




In a normal cell, the <u>β-globin</u> chains are coded by a total of two <u>alleles</u>.;   Thus, there are two main forms of the disease.




* Beta-thalassemia minor (trait): one defective <u>allele</u>

* Beta-thalassemia major (<u>Cooley anemia</u>): two defective <u>alleles</u>

* Sickle cell beta thalassemia: a combination of one defective <u>β-globin</u> <u>allele</u> and one defective <u>HbS</u> <u>allele</u>

* Hemoglobin E/beta thalassemia: a combination of one <u>allele</u> with a <u>hemoglobin E</u> (<u>HbE</u>) variant and one defective <u>β-globin</u> <u>allele</u>. Produces a highly heterogeneous clinical spectrum, and in severe cases patients present with features of <u>beta-thalassemia major</u>.  [[5]](/library/ukXppy)

* Hemoglobin E disease: a condition characterized by homozygosity to the HbE variant. Patients can present with mild features resembling <u>beta-thalassemia minor</u> (i.e., <u>mild anemia</u>).

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>Anemia</u> results from a combination of inefficient <u>erythropoiesis</u> and increased <u>hemolysis</u>. The degree to which both mechanisms contribute to the severity of the disease depends on a patient's exact <u>genotype</u>. [[6]](/library/c1aafj)




* Inefficient <u>erythropoiesis</u> → <u>anemia</u> 

* <u>Beta-thalassemia minor</u> and major: faulty <u>β-globin</u> chain synthesis → ↓ β-chains→ ↑ γ-,δ-chains → ↑ <u>HbF</u> and ↑ <u>HbA2</u>. 
* <u>HbF</u> protects <u>infants</u> up to the age of 6 months, after which <u>HbF</u> production declines and <u>symptoms of anemia</u> appear.

* <u>Alpha-thalassemia intermedia</u> (<u>HbH disease</u>) and <u>alpha-thalassemia major</u> (Bart's disease): faulty <u>α-globin</u> chain synthesis → ↓ α-chains → impaired pairing of α-chains with β-chains and γ-chains→ ↑ free β-, γ-chains → ↑ <u>HbH</u>, ↑ <u>Hb-Bart's</u>

* In minor and minima forms, production of the affected chain is reduced, but enough is produced to prevent <u>severe anemia</u>.

* Increased <u>hemolysis</u>: One of the chains (either α or β) is reduced → compensatory overproduction of other chains → excess <u>globin</u> chains precipitate and form <u>inclusions</u> within <u>RBCs</u> → <u>erythrocyte</u> instability with <u>hemolysis</u>

* <u>Anemia</u> → ↑ <u>erythropoietin</u> → <u>bone marrow</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> and skeletal deformities

---

## Clinical features

### <u>Beta thalassemia</u>




* Minor variant

* No or <u>mild anemia</u>

* Low risk of <u>hemolysis</u> or <u>splenomegaly</u>

* Major variant

* Severe <u>hemolytic anemia</u> that often requires <u>transfusions</u> → <u>secondary iron overload</u> due to <u>hemolysis</u>, <u>transfusion</u>, or both  → secondary <u>hemochromatosis</u>  [[7]](/library/11a2fj)

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Growth retardation

* Skeletal deformities (high forehead, prominent <u>zygomatic bones</u>, and <u>maxilla</u>)

* <u>Transient aplastic crisis</u> (secondary to infection with <u>parvovirus B19</u>) [[8]](/library/CFXq4-)

* <u>Sickle cell beta thalassemia</u>

* Features of <u>sickle cell disease</u>

* Severity depends on the amount of <u>β-globin</u> synthesis.





### <u>Alpha thalassemia</u>




* Silent carrier: typically no <u>anemia</u>

* <u>Alpha-thalassemia trait</u>: : no or <u>mild anemia</u>

* <u>Hemoglobin H disease</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u> and <u>anemia</u> at <u>birth</u>

* Chronic <u>hemolytic</u> <u>anemia</u> that may require <u>transfusions</u> → <u>secondary iron overload</u> due to <u>hemolysis</u>, <u>transfusion</u>, or both → secondary <u>hemochromatosis</u> [[7]](/library/11a2fj)

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Skeletal deformities (less common)

* Compared to thalassemia beta, symptoms in adults are generally less severe.

* <u>Hb-Bart's</u> <u>hydrops fetalis</u> syndrome (most severe variant of <u>alpha thalassemia</u>)

* Intrauterine <u>ascites</u> and <u>hydrops fetalis</u>

* Severe <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Often cardiac and skeletal anomalies

* Incompatible with life (<u>death</u> in utero or shortly after <u>birth</u>)

---

## Diagnosis

### <u>Pretest probability</u> [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)[[10]](/library/dfXoOx)




The presentation of thalassemia is highly variable, ranging from incidental findings to life-threatening forms. Thalassemia is more likely to be diagnosed in patients with the following:




* Suggestive clinical features 

* In <u>infants</u> (usually aged 6–24 months): Consider <u>beta-thalassemia major</u>.

* In children (usually aged 2–6 years): Consider <u>beta-thalassemia minor</u> or alpha/<u>beta-thalassemia</u> intermedia.

* Demographic factors

* <u>Family history</u> of thalassemia

* Asian, African, or Mediterranean ancestry

* Incidental diagnostic findings

* <u>Microcytic hypochromic anemia</u> not explained by other causes or not responsive to supplemental <u>iron</u>

* Antenatal <u>ultrasound</u> showing <u>hydrops fetalis</u>

* Detection of abnormal <u>hemoglobin</u> chains in <u>newborn screening</u>  [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Family history</u> plays an important role in diagnosing patients with clinically silent thalassemia. Consider the possibility of minor forms/traits if a family member is diagnosed with a more severe form.




### Initial investigations [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)[[10]](/library/dfXoOx)




* <u>CBC</u>

* Characteristic finding: <u>microcytic hypochromic anemia</u> (i.e., <u>MCV</u> < 80 fL, <u>MCH</u> < 27 pg/cell) present regardless of <u>Hb</u> level

* <u>Hb</u> levels: variable depending on the subtype

* Other red cell indices

* Normal <u>RDW</u>  [[11]](/library/eoYxaJ)

* Higher <u>RBC count</u> than <u>iron deficiency anemia</u>

* Mentzer index

* <u>MCV</u>/<u>RBC</u> <u>ratio</u> used to differentiate between thalassemia and <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> (<u>IDA</u>)

* A <u>ratio</u> < 13 suggests thalassemia; a <u>ratio</u> > 13 suggests <u>IDA</u>

* See also “<u>Diagnostics of anemia</u>” for further evaluation of <u>microcytosis</u>.

* <u>Hemolysis</u> evaluation: nonimmune-mediated <u>hemolytic anemia</u> 

* ↓ <u>Haptoglobin</u>, ↑ <u>LDH</u>, ↑ <u>reticulocytes</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u> (indirect)

* <u>Coombs test</u>: negative

* <u>Iron studies</u> (particularly <u>ferritin</u>) : expected to be normal in thalassemia

* <u>Peripheral blood smear</u> findings include:

* <u>Target cells</u>

* <u>Teardrop cells</u>

* <u>Anisopoikilocytosis</u>

* <u>HbH</u> <u>inclusion bodies</u>

* <u>Erythroblasts</u>





![Target cells (codocytes)](media/obmpbnll1jnicbbc53bfgzgp.jpg)

![Dacrocytes](media/imr0jcdn1hi6lf4qf7k9kh08.jpg)

Dacrocytes




### Confirmatory diagnostic studies [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)[[10]](/library/dfXoOx)



* Detection of <u>hemoglobin variants</u>

* <u>Hb-electrophoresis</u> (qualitative analysis)

* Automated <u>HPLC</u> (qualitative and quantitative analysis)

* Findings (vary depending on the subtype) 

* <u>Hemoglobin A</u> (and subtypes): <u>hemoglobin A2</u> values are helpful to determine the diagnosis (i.e., to distinguish alpha from <u>beta thalassemia</u>)

* <u>Hemoglobin F</u>: may be elevated in some children and adults with thalassemia

* See “<u>Hemoglobin variants</u>” for findings of other <u>hemoglobinopathies</u>.




| <br>Interpretation of Hb-electrophoresis results for thalassemia [[10]](/library/dfXoOx)[[12]](/library/FVXgwC)[[13]](/library/EOX88y)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Alpha thalassemia</u> |  | <br><u>Beta-thalassemia minor</u>/intermedia/major<br> |
| <br>Minor<br> | <br>Intermedia/<u>HbH disease</u><br> |  |  |
| <u>MCV</u>/<u>MCH</u> | Normal/low | Low | Low |
| <u>HbA2</u> | Normal/low | Normal/low | High |
| <u>HbF</u> | Normal | Normal/high | <br>High <br> |
| <u>HbH</u> | May be present | Present | Absent |





* Genetic studies:  (<u>PCR</u>-based): to determine specific diagnosis and mutations

* <u>Bone marrow aspiration</u> (not routinely indicated)

* Usually performed to rule out other hematologic conditions

* Findings in thalassemia are nonspecific (e.g., reactive <u>hyperplasia</u>).





> [!TIP]
> <u>Beta-thalassemia minor</u> should be strongly suspected if <u>HbA2</u> is > 3.5%. [[12]](/library/FVXgwC)




### Imaging




Imaging is not routinely indicated or required for diagnosis. It can be useful in the evaluation of suspected craniofacial abnormalities and <u>extramedullary hematopoiesis</u>.




* <u>Skull</u> <u>x-ray</u> (AP and <u>lateral</u>)

* Indication: assessment of craniofacial abnormalities

* Findings include:

* High forehead

* Prominent <u>zygomatic bones</u> and <u>maxilla</u> (referred to as “chipmunk facies”)

* <u>Hair-on-end</u> (also known as “crew cut”) sign

* <u>CXR</u>

* Indication: suspected <u>extramedullary hematopoiesis</u> in the thorax

* Findings include:

* <u>Mediastinal</u> or pulmonary masses

* Subperiosteal extension in the <u>ribs</u> (also known as “<u>rib</u> within a <u>rib</u>”)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>spine</u>: helpful to evaluate <u>mass effect</u> symptoms due to <u>extramedullary hematopoietic pseudotumors</u>





![Hair-on-end appearance of the skull](media/tp1dl04tsdu69mhkwwy8uaor.jpg)

Hair-on-end appearance of the skull

![Rib-within-a-rib sign in thalassemia](media/b1k575ockgrogy3nt0k658so.jpg)

Rib-within-a-rib sign in thalassemia

![Spinal epidural mass](media/wpxlh7u8ev7yrv4h3nrtg5pl.jpg)

Spinal epidural mass




> [!NOTE]
> <u>CBC</u> parameters can help differentiate thalassemia minor/trait from <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> (<u>IDA</u>), which is frequently associated with a high <u>RDW</u>, low <u>RBC count</u>, and low <u>MCV</u>, typically occurring once <u>Hb</u> is < 10 g/dL. In thalassemia, <u>microcytosis</u> is always present regardless of <u>Hb</u> level, and <u>RDW</u> is normal to increased. Also, <u>RBC count</u> is higher and <u>MCV</u> is lower than in <u>IDA</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Low <u>ferritin</u> suggests <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> and patients should receive <u>iron</u> supplementation. Suspect thalassemia if there is no significant response after three months. [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)[[10]](/library/dfXoOx)

---

## Management

* All patients

* Patient education and <u>genetic counseling</u>.

* <u>Screening tests</u> for relatives

* Thalassemia minor

* Usually no treatment required

* Episodic <u>folic acid supplementation</u> may be indicated (e.g., during <u>pregnancy</u>, acute infections)

* Thalassemia major and intermedia

* <u>Transfusion</u> therapy (<u>erythrocyte</u> concentrates) 

* Indication (for <u>transfusion</u>-dependent thalassemias): <u>Hb</u> < 7 g/dL or marked clinical symptoms

* Target: <u>Hb</u> 9–10 g/dL

* Surveillance and treatment of complications

* <u>Iron overload diseases</u>: <u>chelating agents</u>, e.g., deferasirox, indicated when <u>iron</u> accumulation reaches toxic levels

* Other complications: e.g., <u>gallstones</u>, <u>asplenia</u>, <u>extramedullary hematopoietic pseudotumors</u>

* Select patients 

* <u>Splenectomy</u>

* Potentially curative treatment

* <u>Stem cell transplantation</u>: <u>allogenic HSCT</u>

* <u>Gene therapy</u>





References: [[9]](/library/WfXPOx)[[10]](/library/dfXoOx)

## Special patient groups

### Thalassemia in pregnancy [[16]](/library/joc_bW0)[[17]](/library/PocWXW0)[[18]](/library/4oc3XW0)[[19]](/library/kocmXW0)



* Overview

* Most patients with thalassemia may suffer from <u>infertility</u> and require <u>assisted reproductive technology</u> to achieve <u>pregnancy</u>.

* Spontaneous <u>fertility</u> may occur in patients who have successfully undergone <u>iron chelation therapy</u> and <u>blood transfusion</u>.  [[20]](/library/WocPaW0)

* <u>Pregnancies</u> in patients with thalassemia should be planned, as they are considered high-risk for both the mother and fetus.

* Preconception <u>genetic counseling</u>, close antenatal monitoring and screening, and <u>intrapartum</u> and postpartum management are highly recommended.

* A multidisciplinary team, including a hematologist, cardiologist, endocrinologist, and <u>gynecologist</u>, should be involved in the management of pregnant patients with thalassemia.




#### <u>Fertility</u> assessment and management




* Screening for thalassemia

* <u>Hemoglobinopathy</u> screening should be offered to women with unknown <u>hemoglobinopathy</u> status and <u>normocytic</u> or <u>microcytic anemia</u>.

* Partner screening for thalassemia carrier status

* Not a carrier for thalassemia: Follow protocols for spontaneous <u>conception</u>, <u>ovulation induction</u> (e.g., <u>gonadotropins</u>, <u>clomiphene citrate</u>), or <u>in vitro fertilization</u>.

* Carrier of <u>alpha thalassemia</u>: Offer <u>preimplantation genetic testing</u> and <u>in vitro fertilization</u>.

* Partner has <u>thalassemia trait</u>: Advise patients to use donor <u>gametes</u> or a <u>sperm</u> donor.

* If both partners have thalassemia or <u>thalassemia trait</u>: Offer <u>genetic counseling</u> prior to <u>conception</u>. After successful <u>conception</u>, the fetus will undergo thalassemia screening using <u>chorionic villus sampling</u> or <u>amniocentesis</u>.

* If both partners have thalassemia major: Consider alternatives including adoption.

* <u>Preconception screening</u> and review: The most important factors to consider during a <u>fertility</u> assessment are cardiac and <u>liver function</u>, and risk of <u>vertical transmission</u> of viral diseases. Diagnostics include:

* <u>Ovarian reserve</u>: <u>anti-Müllerian hormone</u> levels

* <u>CBC</u> (<u>MCH</u>, <u>MCV</u>) and <u>RBC indices</u>

* <u>Hb electrophoresis</u>

* <u>Iron studies</u>

* Cardiac function: <u>echocardiogram</u>, <u>electrocardiogram</u>, T2 star <u>cardiac MRI</u>

* <u>Liver function</u>: <u>liver function</u> tests, <u>liver elastography</u>, <u>liver</u> and <u>gallbladder</u> <u>ultrasound</u>

* <u>Bone density</u>: <u>DEXA scan</u>, <u>vitamin D</u>, <u>calcium</u> levels

* Endocrine function: <u>thyroid function tests</u>, blood <u>glucose</u> levels

* <u>Coagulation studies</u>: <u>PT</u>, <u>INR</u>, <u>protein C</u>, <u>protein S</u>, <u>homocysteine</u>, <u>thrombophilia panel</u>

* Viral infection screening: <u>HBV</u>, <u>HCV</u>, <u>HIV</u>

* Screening for <u>RBC</u> <u>antibodies</u>

* <u>Medication review</u>: <u>folic acid</u>, <u>vitamin D</u>, <u>calcium</u> supplementation, <u>oral iron</u> <u>chelators</u>





#### Antepartum screening




* Evaluation

* Cardiac function tests each trimester

* <u>Gestational diabetes</u> screening at 16 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* <u>Fetal growth monitoring</u>: serial fetal biometric ultrasounds starting from 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Assessment of <u>splenomegaly</u>

* <u>Iron chelation</u> treatment: should be adjusted and closely monitored during <u>pregnancy</u>

* <u>Deferoxamine</u>: used in the second and third trimesters

* Deferasirox and deferiprone: must be discontinued 3 months prior to <u>conception</u>

* <u>Transfusions</u>: should aim to maintain <u>hemoglobin</u> > 10 g/dL to prevent intrauterine <u>fetal growth restriction</u>





#### <u>Intrapartum</u> and postpartum management




* Although vaginal delivery is possible, patients usually require <u>cesarean delivery</u>, as those with thalassemia have an increased <u>incidence</u> of <u>cephalopelvic disproportion</u>.

* <u>Breastfeeding</u> should not be discouraged.

* Resume <u>iron chelation therapy</u>, if eligible.

* <u>Deferoxamine</u> can be resumed immediately postpartum.

* The use of deferasirox and deferiprone should be delayed until the patient has stopped <u>breastfeeding</u>.

* Continue <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation.

* <u>Thromboprophylaxis</u> with <u>LMW heparin</u>

* Discuss <u>contraception</u> options (i.e., <u>progesterone-only pill</u> or barrier methods).





#### Complications




* Maternal

* Cardiac failure

* <u>Alloimmunization</u>

* <u>Thrombosis</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Hyperparathyroidism</u>

* Fetal

* Growth restriction

* <u>Prematurity</u>

* Transmission of <u>hepatitis B</u>, <u>hepatitis C</u>, and/or <u>HIV</u>
